analysis.one_liner: Has the government manufacture COVID-19 drugs, tests, and protective gear, overriding drug patents with paid compensation.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in February 2021 and died there without a vote, without a hearing, and with only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a government office inside the Department of Health and Human Services that makes COVID-19 medicines, vaccines, diagnostic test materials, and protective gear — and, for drugs and supplies in shortage, other needed medicines too. To do that, it could have taken over the right to manufacture patented products by issuing licenses over the owners' objection, with the owners paid a capped royalty. COVID-19 products would have been given free to federal, state, tribal, and local health programs and sold at cost to everyone else, with all prices posted publicly. The office would have been barred from employing former drug-company lobbyists or executives of drug manufacturers under federal enforcement settlements.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and health programs that depend on scarce COVID-19 treatments, tests, and protective gear — including the Indian Health Service and tribal health programs, which are named for free provision. Hospitals and nursing and home-care workers get a guaranteed domestic supply of masks, gowns, and N95s. People who rely on drugs prone to shortage get a backup public manufacturer selling at cost-based prices, and taxpayers save when health programs buy at cost instead of list price.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, health programs, and pandemic supply chains

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders HHS to begin manufacturing N95 masks, surgical gowns, test swabs and reagents, and shortage drugs used in severe COVID-19 cases within one month of enactment, and to build vaccine manufacturing facilities so production can scale up immediately after approval [S3].

It would provide COVID-19 products at no cost to federal, state, local, and Native health programs and other domestic health care providers, and sell them at cost to commercial and international buyers, with every price posted publicly [S2] [S3].

The Secretary could issue involuntary licenses letting the office make and sell patented drugs, biological products, and devices — and use the owners' clinical trial data and manufacturing know-how — while paying rights holders a royalty capped at the pharmaceutical industry's average royalty rate reported to the IRS [S2] [S3].

The office itself would be off-limits for six years to former registered drug manufacturer lobbyists and to former senior executives of drug manufacturers operating under federal settlements or enforcement actions [S3].
The HHS Inspector General would audit at least one of every three manufacturing contracts, make each review public, and recommend fixes to Congress when prices are unreasonable [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug and vaccine makers, whose exclusive patent and data rights could be overridden with a capped royalty rather than negotiated license fees. Taxpayers, who fund the office, its facilities, and the free distribution of products. Contract manufacturers that win government work would have to accept government-set reasonable pricing.

drawbacks.text: The royalty cap means patent holders could not negotiate market-rate license fees; companies argue that forced licensing below market rates weakens the financial reward that motivates investment in new drugs and vaccines [S3].

The bill commits the federal government to building and running pharmaceutical plants and producing vaccines and drugs on fixed one-month timelines, a capability the government has never had at scale, with no specified funding ceiling — appropriations were left open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary') [S3].

Free provision applies only to health programs and designated providers; consumers in the commercial market would pay cost — which could still be above what insurers or manufacturers would otherwise charge for some generics [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: During an active pandemic with N95 and testing shortages, the benefit of guaranteed public manufacturing and free distribution to health programs would have been large, and the bill built in real guardrails — a capped, market-benchmarked royalty rather than uncompensated seizure, IG audits, public pricing, and a revolving-door ban on drug lobbyists. The honest costs are the open-ended taxpayer price of building public manufacturing capacity and the risk that forced licensing, if used aggressively over time, would erode drugmakers' incentive to invest in new products. The design tries to thread that needle; whether it would have worked in practice was never tested, because the bill was never debated.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health Subcommittee from February 2021 until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Pandemic Emergency Manufacturing Act of 2021 on February 2, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 117th Congress [S5].
It ended the Congress with one cosponsor, a Democrat, and never received a hearing or vote in committee or on the House floor [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical and vaccine patent holders are better off: they kept sole control of their patents, clinical trial data, and manufacturing know-how, and faced no government competitor selling their products at cost. Taxpayers also avoided the open-ended cost of building public drug manufacturing plants.

for.name: Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never granted it a hearing, markup, or vote; the Health Subcommittee held it from February 3, 2021 onward.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll call exists; the bill's entire recorded support was two House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor.

industries.note: The government could override their patents, clinical trial data, and manufacturing know-how with a royalty capped at the industry's average IRS-reported rate, then sell their products at cost or give them away — eliminating monopoly pricing on affected products. Their interest ran against the bill's free and at-cost supply for health programs.

Public manufacturing of masks, gowns, and face shields would compete with their sales, but they could also win government manufacturing contracts — which require reasonable pricing, and US-made components were prioritized.

industries.industry: Generic drug makers and active ingredient suppliers
industries.note: The office would manufacture active pharmaceutical ingredients that are scarce or vulnerable to disruption and sell them to other manufacturers, explicitly to make it easier for new competitors to enter the market.
